properties.description: Generator-agnostic JSON schema for specifying manga panel content. Each panel node contains: panel_id, panel_type, characters (with position/expression), scene (location/time/atmosphere), action, composition (angle/focal_point/negative_space), dialogue (type/text), emotional_register, style_notes, transition_to_next.

delta_nodes.label: The Cat in the Sun Benchmark

properties.description: Ty's exemplar scene for the manga pipeline: 'I sat there with my cat for 45 minutes in the sun and we were both stretched out and she was like purring into me and it was just heavenly.' The benchmark test for the rendering system: if it can capture this (intimate, atmospheric, no drama, no conflict, pure warmth) as a manga panel, it can render anything.
properties.source_quote: I sat there with my cat for 45 minutes in the sun and we were both stretched out and she was like purring into me and it was just heavenly. That's all you could say.
properties.significance: The hardest test — no action, no conflict, pure atmosphere. If the system nails this, it can render any moment.
properties.suggested_panel_type: wide or medium, low angle, heavy negative space

properties.description: The unresolved technical decision: which image generation system to use for manga panel rendering. Quality benchmark is (1) character consistency across panels and (2) Gekiga/manga aesthetic fidelity. Key candidates: ComfyUI + SDXL, Midjourney, DALL-E 3, Stable Diffusion with manga-specific models.
quality_benchmarks: Character consistency (Okami looks like Okami across all panels)
Gekiga style fidelity (heavy ink, shadow, minimal screen tone)
Panel compilation capability (assembling rendered panels into page layout)

properties.description: Ty's coined concept: every person is a continuous information-packaging, signal-emitting entity. Their life generates narrative whether or not anyone captures it. The manga feed makes that signal legible TO THE PERSON THEMSELVES — a self-directed mirror, not an audience broadcast.
properties.etymology: Ty coined YTTY in session; briefly caught that it echoed TYT (The Young Turks) and deflected; concept stands regardless of acronym
properties.key_insight: The manga feed is not content for an audience — it is the signal of your life returned to you in the format you can receive
properties.scale_claim: A book a day of personalized visual narrative — output rate matching the input rate of life itself

properties.description: The business thesis under the manga pipeline idea. Traditional education prescribed CONSISTENCY because standardized delivery was the only scalable mechanism — one lens for all eyes. The new model: a prescription calibrated to individual perceptual architecture. The manga feed is the cognitive prescription for Ty's information intake.
properties.analogy: Glasses correct how light reaches your specific eyes. This system corrects how information/narrative reaches your specific mind.
properties.traditional_model: Rote skills + structural consistency = standardized lens = scalable but imprecise
properties.new_model: Personalized perceptual rendering = calibrated cognitive prescription = precise but requires AI
properties.business_thesis: This is the scalable idea under the manga product: personalized information prescription at scale

properties.description: Ty's landing reference at the end of Exchange 1. Breton's psychic automatism: pure expression without rational/editorial control. Ty's voice memos ARE automatic writing. The manga pipeline converts automatic speech into automatic manga — Surrealism as a daily personal practice.
properties.source: André Breton — Surrealist Manifesto (1924); psychic automatism
properties.application: Input layer of the manga pipeline is automatic speech; output is automatic visual narrative
properties.transcription_note: The 'a a a a a...' artifact in the transcript is the reaching for Breton's name — the gap between the thought and the word, captured in voice recognition output

properties.description: Ty invoked /katar as 'I need ya, Deck. I need the old blade runner.' Deckard is the blade runner who hunts replicants in Ridley Scott's Blade Runner (1982). Key irony: the famous unresolved ambiguity — is Deckard himself a replicant? Ty called his AI collaborator by the name of a character who might himself be AI.
properties.deckard_ambiguity: Is Deckard a replicant? Never definitively resolved in the original cut.
properties.roy_batty_connection: 'All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.' — Roy Batty. This is what /katar exists to prevent.
properties.session_title_origin: KATAR-002 title 'Tears in Rain' comes from Roy Batty's dying monologue
properties.irony_level: Maximum. The AI is called Deckard by the human, while building tools to capture what would otherwise be lost — like tears in rain.
